sermon.title: Cruel and Unusual Punishments
sermon.speaker: Pastor David G. Kincer
sermon.summary: In “Cruel and Unusual Punishments,” Pastor David G. Kincer quotes the Supreme Court’s 1958 “evolving standards of decency” line, reviews U.S. penalties (prison, parole, probation, restitution, fines, death), and contrasts Bible restitution, stripes, limited servitude, refuge cities and death for murder—with no OT prisons. He argues some modern sentences are unusually light for violent crimes named in the transcript, and from 1 Timothy and Deuteronomy that punishment should be public so others fear and turn from evil.
sermon.transcript_source: This transcript comes from YouTube’s automatic English captions, which supply the timing and the words. Punctuation, capitalization and paragraphing were added by hand, and obvious caption errors were corrected; his wording was not rewritten. “[unclear]” marks a word or name that was not clear. HIGHLY SENSITIVE: names real perpetrators and victims of rape, child sexual abuse, torture-murder and mutilation (on-screen cases); kept in the transcript only, not in short answers/FAQ. Homosexual relationship in one teen murder case kept as spoken. Caption fixes: an→and; giddy→guilty; hard yourself→hired; acts handle→axe handle; wither fist→with her fist; buried our life→buried her alive; peace→piece; president→present. Prison/parole/probation counts (2.3M / 800k / 2.5M), 15,000 murders / 35 executions in 2014, and case details are his figures—not verified. Trop v. Dulles (1958 citizenship) framed as he tells it.

chunks.section_question: What did the Supreme Court say about cruel and unusual punishment in 1958?
chunks.short_answer: He quotes that the Eighth Amendment must draw its meaning from the evolving standards of decency of a maturing society, and tells of a half-day deserter who lost citizenship—the Court called that cruel and unusual for that crime.
chunks.text: Today we’re going to look at the issue of the Eighth Amendment of the Constitution: what is cruel and unusual punishment? What is cruel and unusual punishment that the Constitution says we cannot punish people with? The Supreme Court in 1958 made this statement: the Eighth Amendment must draw its meaning from the evolving standards of decency that mark the progress of a maturing society. A soldier had deserted for half a day, came back, turned himself in; he was sent to the brig, he was discharged with an undesirable discharge, and then they took his citizenship away. And the Supreme Court said no—the Eighth Amendment—that is cruelty and that is an unusual severe punishment for that crime. So remember they said this statement: the Eighth Amendment must draw its meaning from the evolving standards

chunks.section_question: What punishments does he say America uses?
chunks.short_answer: He lists prison (about 2.3 million), parole (800,000+), probation (2.5 million), restitution (which he doubts is really collected), and community service at a charity for so many hours.
chunks.text: of a progressing mature society. In America we have several punishments. We have prison, and we have 2.3 million people in prison, and we have eight-tenths of a million—800,000 or more—on parole from prison. And then we have the probation: you know, first-timer, we’ll put you on probation, you know, you just check in with us and be a nice guy. Two and a half million are on probation in America. Then you have restitution. And honestly, all the people I know, I have never heard one of them thieves having to pay back even what they stole plus the loan added to it, so I don’t know about this one, but they say it’s a law. Community service: so you pick your charity, you did a bad thing like some famous people do, so you pick a charity and you go work in that charity for so many hours—that is your punishment.

chunks.section_question: How often is the death penalty used, in his figures?
chunks.short_answer: He puts a question mark on it: 15,000 murders in 2014 and only 35 executions—doesn’t sound carried out in a progressive mature society. Bible civil penalties he lists: restitution, fines, and at most 40 stripes.
chunks.text: Then you have fines where you pay a dollar amount for your punishment and then you’re just free to go. And then you have the death penalty—and I got a question mark there, because there were 15,000 murders in 2014 and only 35 people were executed with the death penalty. Doesn’t sound like it’s carried out in this progressive and a decent mature society. chunks.section_question: Does Bible “servitude” mean slavery, in his teaching?
chunks.short_answer: He says no: debtors hired themselves out up to six years to pay bills—not slavery. Refuge cities protected accidental killers from the avenger of blood until trial. Courts could beat bullies (39 stripes to stay under 40).
chunks.text: So everybody beat 39 times so they didn’t go over the mark. And that was over a physical dispute: you’re a bully, you’re going around beating up 11-, 12-, 13-, 14-year-old guys and you’re 18, 19, 20, or your threesome in your little group is beating up people in the community—then the courts can beat you. All right. Servitude is very misunderstood in the Bible. Everybody that attacks the Bible says that slavery—that is not slavery. That is: you went into debt, or you had a bad business adventure, you couldn’t pay your bills, so you went and hired yourself out to someone for six years, or in that period of six years, to pay off that debt. It couldn’t last any more than six years, so it’s not slavery at all. Refuge cities were for people who accidentally killed someone: your axe handle, your axe flew off and hurt your neighbor and killed him, and so you could run to the city of refuge so the avenger of blood, the family, couldn’t come and kill you until you had a trial and found innocent.

chunks.section_question: What counts as cruel and unusual in the Bible?
chunks.short_answer: He says the OT has no prison sentences—dealt with that day. Cruel examples: death for theft, death without trial by a mob, and torture (totally forbidden). Jail today is like a city of refuge until trial.
chunks.text: And then you had murder and you had the death penalty. And over here we have little symbols of that: death penalty was carried out by stoning or a sword; this is the whipping lash; and a jail is our city of refuge today—you go to jail to protect you from people and protect society from you until you’ve had a trial and found guilty. There are no prisons in the Old Testament laws—no prison sentences at all. Everything was dealt with that day, at that time, at that moment, and done and decided. So cruel and unusual punishment in the Bible would be death for a theft: you kill a person because they steal your horse—the Bible would say that was cruel and unusual punishment for that crime. Death without a trial: the mob, they accuse you of something, they think you’re guilty, and they just take you and they hang you and they stone you—that’s cruel and unusual in the Bible. chunks.short_answer: After describing violent crimes against children and teens (details in the transcript), he asks why the offender was free to harm an innocent girl, and notes another offender got probation then short sentences after repeat rapes.
chunks.text: Takes her to his trailer where his sister and her lover lived—and you can see all three of them are on drugs. I mean, come on, anybody can tell something’s wrong there. And he rapes this nine-year-old girl, tore her vagina from the rape, put her in a closet to stay there all day without food till he got home. And my point is this: why was he back in society to harm this innocent girl? Secondly, we got Josh up there. He got a teenage girl drunk, 13 years old, intoxicated, and raped her, and he was given probation. Two years later, after he got off probation, he got a 14-year-old girl drunk and raped her, and he served one year.

chunks.short_answer: He asks whether treating the criminal with such decency that serious crime has no real penalty is the direction the Court says we are heading, and notes one victim survived after hikers found her.

chunks.section_question: What is the Bible purpose of punishment?
chunks.short_answer: From 1 Timothy 5:20, rebuke sinners before all that others may fear. From Deuteronomy 17:12, put away evil so all hear and fear and do no more presumptuously.
chunks.text: Is this the direction we’re going, where the criminal is treated with such decency that there is no real penalty for a serious crime? Is this—for the Supreme Court says we are heading—two hikers came by. She was walking with her hands up trying to keep the bleeding down. Just happened two hikers came by and took the girl to the hospital, and she’s alive today. Purpose of punishment: 1 Timothy 5:20, them that sin rebuke before all, that others also may fear. Deuteronomy 17:12: you shall put away the evil from Israel; all the people will hear and fear and do no more presumptuously.

chunks.section_question: What does he call cruel and unusual punishment today?
chunks.short_answer: From Deuteronomy 19:19 he says punishment should be publicized to deter. Cruel and unusual, to him, is authorities not punishing and publicizing, not informing citizens of destructive results, and missing morals and self-control—the puzzle piece—not decency.
chunks.text: So penalizing is for deterring crime. Deuteronomy 19:19: put evil away from your midst, and those that remain shall hear and fear and shall from henceforth commit no more such evil. Punishment is to be publicized, to be public, to cause those that are coming up behind to stay away from a life of crime. Now, cruel and unusual punishment is civil authorities not discouraging future criminals by punishing present criminals and publicizing it; civil authorities not informing uninformed citizens of immoral behaviors’ destructive and life-ending results; and the conclusion that no morals, no knowledge of morals, lack of self-control is the missing social puzzle piece in America. And it is not decency when we do not punish the criminal for the proper crime.

faqs.question: What are “evolving standards of decency”?
faqs.answer: He quotes the 1958 Court: the Eighth Amendment must draw its meaning from the evolving standards of decency that mark the progress of a maturing society.

faqs.question: How many people does he say are in prison or on supervision?
faqs.answer: About 2.3 million in prison, 800,000+ on parole, and 2.5 million on probation.

faqs.question: Why beat 39 times instead of 40?
faqs.answer: He says the Bible allows at most 40 stripes, so they beat 39 so they didn’t go over the mark.

faqs.question: What were cities of refuge for?
faqs.answer: For someone who accidentally killed another (axe head flying off) so the avenger of blood couldn’t kill them before a trial.

faqs.question: Were there prisons in Old Testament law?
faqs.answer: He says no prison sentences at all; everything was dealt with that day, at that time, and decided.

faqs.question: Does the Bible allow torture?
faqs.answer: He says torture is totally forbidden in the Bible—no torture at all.

faqs.question: What penalty did a false witness get?
faqs.answer: Whatever penalty they sought for the accused was done to them—if they sought stoning, they were stoned.

faqs.question: Why rebuke before all, per 1 Timothy 5:20?
faqs.answer: So that others also may fear.
